title: Mutually unbiased bases: common states, completion, and extension obstructions
abstract: Which pure states give uniform outcomes in several mutually unbiased measurements, and when can they form another measurement basis? We distinguish common unbiased states, their orthonormal completion, and further extension. For a displayed phase-deformed Fourier pair in dimension $2m$, a clock symmetry and skew antiunitary complete every prescribed common unbiased state to an explicit orthonormal basis. In dimension six, an amplitude-profile obstruction proves strong unextendibility of a given mutually unbiased triple when its original third-basis rays are invariant under the ternary clock. We give an exact nonproduct example and an application to a companion whose columns are localized at single Fourier frequencies. For every exact Hadamard matrix in a specified closed entrywise neighborhood of a fixed reference matrix, the coordinate and Hadamard bases have exactly 48 common unbiased rays but no third measurement basis, with a quantitative lower bound on the squared Gram defect of every six-column candidate.   We also study auxiliary complex equations for common states, retaining algebraic multiplicities. For a flat unitary of order six with all $3\times3$ minors nonzero, the projective ray scheme is finite; each singular two-minor contributes two reduced isolated boundary points, and the affine coordinate algebra is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$. In every order, a critical-algebra identity preserves multiplicities; in dimension six it gives finiteness for a fixed phase fibre. Specialization over a discrete valuation ring controls complete reciprocal-orthogonal collections. A nonphysical Tao/Potts collection separates algebraic from physical solutions. These results do not determine the global maximum number of mutually unbiased bases or classify all triples.
summary: This paper deeply explores the mathematical structure of Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUBs) by analyzing common unbiased states and the conditions required for their completion into full measurement bases. Using advanced algebraic geometry, the authors establish constructive theorems for certain systems while also deriving specific obstructions that limit the number of such bases in higher dimensions. It provides fundamental theoretical constraints on quantum measurement theory.
main_problem: The paper investigates the mathematical constraints governing common unbiased states and the conditions under which a set of such states can be completed to form a full orthonormal measurement basis in quantum systems.
main_result: The authors provide explicit constructions showing that for specific Fourier pairs, common unbiased states can be completed to an orthonormal basis, while also deriving obstructions (e.g., in dimension six) that prove strong unextendibility for certain configurations.
method: The work employs advanced algebraic and geometric techniques, analyzing projective ray schemes, affine coordinate algebras, and utilizing complex equations derived from quantum measurement theory.
model_or_system: The model is abstract quantum measurement theory, focusing on pure states represented as rays in a complex Hilbert space, and measurements defined by orthonormal bases (like the Fourier or Hadamard bases).
key_observables: Common unbiased states, the Gram defect of candidate bases, and the structure of the projective ray scheme.
important_parameters: The dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space (especially $d=6$), and the neighborhood size ($\epsilon$) around reference matrices.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on specific, highly structured input bases (like phase-deformed Fourier pairs) or the assumption of small perturbations around known exact matrices.
figures_summary: Not specified; the notes describe mathematical theorems and structural proofs rather than figure content.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining common unbiased states and the problem of completion, to presenting specific constructive theorems (e.g., for Fourier pairs), followed by detailed algebraic analyses of constraints (finiteness results) and specific dimensional obstructions.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed here—linking algebraic geometry to the existence of quantum measurement bases—provides deep structural insights into the limits of quantum information processing.
